newsitem.title: UK: Gold prices sit out the German row.
newsitem.headline: Gold prices sit out the German row.

text.p: The price of gold was itself stubbornly unmoved amid the turmoil over what Germany does with its reserves.

Bullion analysts differed on whether implications of the row about that between the German government and the Bundesbank would help restore gold - languishing in recent years - to a status as an investor "safe haven".
The gold price at the 0930 GMT London fixing was $345.70 an ounce which was up from $342.80 on Wednesday.

But dealers were unsure how much that reflected news late Wednesday that the Bundesbank rejected a government plan to revalue German reserves, to use the paper profit to plug gaps in the 1997 budget and bring Germany within criteria for European Monetary Union (EMU).
Andy Smith, bullion analyst at Union Bank of Switzerland, said there could be positives for gold, against a backdrop of present fears that European central banks may sell gold to meet EMU rules.

"Either there's a postponement (of EMU) until this issue is sorted out, which is good for gold as a relief factor from (bank) sales. Or if it does go ahead on some balance sheet massaging basis, the need for gold sales is reduced..." Smith said.
Meantime the Bonn government attack on the Bundesbank "has raised investor fears generally about inflation outlooks, which is positive".

But Smith said it was difficult to work out an investor strategy for the next three-to-six months and what would be a viable portfolio while the German argument rages, although "there may be a basic argument for gold as a step out from all this".

Other market-watchers differed, arguing that if Germany managed to fudge EMU rules, inflation could rise and the new Euro currency would be weakened, giving scope for trading currency and bonds against it and Eurobonds.
That might be preferable to bringing gold into the portfolio, said Ted Arnold, markets analyst at Merrill Lynch.
"Gold has been such a dog for the past 10 or 20 years, I can't imagine anybody putting money into it," he said.
He added that capital markets were adept at punishing governments who let inflation rip by selling their currencies and bond markets short.
"If the Euro is weakened it could encourage the European Central Bank to sell gold into the market to prop it up," he said.
Another analyst said the uncertainty in Germany over the next few months would not help gold.
"If the Bundesbank wins on this and there seems to be a chance that it will, it will keep the debate going on gold reserves and that will not be good for the market," he said.
He added that investors would remain cautious but there might be some reallocation of assets into gold from currencies if foreign exchange markets became turbulent.

But regardless of the German outcome, it did not lessen the possibility of central banks selling gold reserves before an ECB was established and had jurisdiction over reserve portfolios, this analyst said

Germany would be the last major European Union power to value its gold in a way that brings it closer to market prices. Only Luxembourg with 12 tonnes in its reserves and Sweden with 187 currently value their reserves at figures unrelated to the market.
